20 Hidden Gems in Washington State You’ll Actually Want to Visit

Share
Share on Facebook
Tweet
Tweet this
Pin
Pin this

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 17:01
Instaread

Everyone knows Washington for Mount Rainier and Olympic National Park, and honestly, they earn their reputation. But they can’t be counted as hidden gems in Washington state. After living in Seattle for over a decade and building a whole career around exploring the Pacific Northwest like a local, I can tell you the real magic is off the beaten path. The famous parks are gorgeous…and they’re also packed with tour buses by 10nAM.

I’ve spent years wandering the state on my own weekends and researching it as a licensed travel agent, and the places below are the ones I actually send friends to. These aren’t the big-name parks everyone already visits. They’re the lesser-known corners of Washington state: the quiet islands, the sleepy towns, and the desert waterfalls that most travelers drive right past.

Consider this your local’s treasure trove. I’ve packed in the practical stuff too, so you’ll know how to get there, what pass you need, and the best season to go.

20 hidden Gems in Washington State

Here’s the running list of my favorite under-the-radar hidden gems in Washington state, sorted so you can build a whole road trip around them. I’ll keep adding to this over time, so make sure to bookmark it and save it to Pinterest to keep up!

North Cascades National Park

website | area: North Cascades National Park (get directions) | best for: hiking and dramatic scenery

I always tell people this is the least crowded of the Pacific Northwest national parks, and it’s wild that more people don’t know about it. You get jagged, glacier-carved peaks and that impossibly turquoise water at Diablo Lake, minus the Rainier crowds.

Pro tip: Drive the North Cascades Highway (SR 20) and stop at the Diablo Lake Overlook. The highway typically closes in winter due to snow, so summer and early fall are your window. I prefer fall because that’s when you can hunt for magical larch trees.

Mt. Baker Recreation Area

website | area: Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest (get directions) | best for: hiking, alpine scenery, and winter recreation

If you want stunning views without fighting a permit lottery, Mt. Baker is your spot. The Artist Point area at the end of SR 542 gives you one of the best mountain panoramas in the Pacific Northwest, with Baker on one side and Mount Shuksan on the other.

Pro tip: The road to Artist Point opens late (often not until late July) because of snowpack. Check conditions before you drive up.

Lake Quinault and its waterfalls

website | area: Quinault Rain Forest (get directions) | best for: rainforest hikes, waterfalls, and scenic drives

Tucked into the rainforest on the Olympic Peninsula, Lake Quinault is a lush, mossy dream, and it stays quiet compared to the big park entrances. I love the short waterfall walks around the lake, plus the historic Lake Quinault Lodge for a cozy afternoon by the fire. It’s one of the best lakes in Washington that few people talk about.

Washington coast beaches

area: Long Beach Peninsula & Southwest Washington Coast (get directions) | best for: beachcombing, sunsets, and wide sandy beaches

Skip the crowds and head to the Washington coast. There are a bunch of small towns dotting the shore. Seabrook is a charming planned beach town that’s great for families, Long Beach gives you miles of flat sand you can actually drive on, and Westport is your spot for surfing and fresh-off-the-boat seafood.

If you want a deeper dive on the coast, I’ve got a whole guide to Washington State attractions worth stealing for your trip. And bonus, it’s near Olympic National Park if you want to squeeze in that iconic attraction, too.

Mt. St. Helens

website | area: Mount St. Helens National Volcanic Monument (get directions) | best for: volcanic landscapes, hiking, and scenic viewpoints

There’s something humbling about standing where a volcano blew its top in 1980. The Johnston Ridge area gives you dramatic views straight into the crater, and the whole landscape feels otherworldly as it slowly comes back to life. Plus it’s near Ape Cave, a cool volcanic tunnel system created by the blast.

Pro tip: Some viewpoints and roads have limited seasonal access and construction, so check current status before you commit to the drive.

Columbia River Gorge

website | area: Columbia River Gorge National Scenic area (get directions) | best for: waterfalls, scenic drives, and hiking

The Columbia River Gorge is one of those places that feels like it belongs on a postcard, and the Washington side stays quieter than Oregon’s. Waterfalls, wind-carved cliffs, and killer hiking, all within easy reach of a wine stop.

I have a bunch of guide’s to the area, so use them to plot your trip:

  • Everything You Need to Know About the Gorge
  • Best Itinerary for Exploring Columbia Gorge
  • My Favorite Gorge Wineries
  • Map of the Best Gorge Waterfalls

Hood Canal

website | area: Olympic Peninsula (get directions) | best for: oysters, kayaking, and scenic waterfront views

Hood Canal is where I go for oysters and quiet. This fjord-like arm of Puget Sound is dotted with tiny towns, shellfish farms, and low-key waterfront spots that feel a world away from the city. If you plan to harvest your own shellfish, check current Washington state shellfish safety and licensing rules first.

Stevens Pass and Snoqualmie Pass hikes

website | area: Central Cascades (get directions) | best for: alpine lakes, mountain views, and day hikes

The passes are packed with incredible alpine trails, and most out-of-towners never think to stop there on their way over the mountains. Lakes, wildflowers, and ridge lines are all within an hour or two of Seattle at Stevens Pass along highway 2 and Snoqualmie Pass along I-90. Bonus: If you like downhill or cross-country skiing, some of the best Washington state ski resorts are there.

I have a whole hiking guide baked into my roundup of things to do in Washington State if you want specific trails to target. Or check out this guide on hikes near Seattle.

Palouse Falls State Park

website | area: Southeastern Washington (get directions) | best for: waterfall views, photography, and dramatic canyon scenery

Palouse Falls is the official state waterfall with a 200-foot plunge into a raw Ice Age canyon with almost no forest in sight. Palouse Falls State Park Heritage Site is a 94-acre day-use park with dramatic views of the official state waterfall. A few honest logistics, because this spot is remote. 

Trailers and RVs aren’t allowed, so you won’t see throngs of overnighters. Also, the majority of the park doesn’t have cell phone service. Palouse Falls is far away from nearby cities, amenities, and first responders, so plan ahead to help make your trip a success.

One safety note: all trails into the canyon and base of Palouse Falls are permanently closed. Venturing beyond designated viewing areas and trails at the park is prohibited.

Snoqualmie and North Bend

website | area: Snoqualmie Valley (get directions) | best for: waterfalls, hiking, and mountain scenery

These twin towns at the foot of the Cascades are pure charm, and yes, Twin Peaks fans, this is your pilgrimage. Snoqualmie Falls is the obvious draw, but the walkable downtowns, diner pie, and easy trailheads make it a great low-effort day trip from Seattle. Use my guide on the best things to do in Snoqualmie to ensure you hit all the best stops!

Snohomish

website | area: Snohomish County (get directions) | best for: historic downtown, antique shopping, and small-town charm

Antique lovers, this is your town. Historic downtown Snohomish is a walkable stretch of shops, cafes, and old brick buildings that make for a lovely slow afternoon. Give yourself time to browse First Street rather than rushing through, since half the fun is popping into whatever antique store or local shop catches your eye.

There’s a lot more to do in Snohomish beyond the historic downtown. Check out my guide on all the best things to do for more ideas of hidden gems in Washington state.

Edmonds

website | area: Puget Sound (get directions) | best for: waterfront views, beaches, and a walkable downtown

Edmonds is one of my favorite easy escapes north of Seattle. It’s a walkable waterfront town with a ferry dock, sweet little restaurants, and sunset views over Puget Sound that rival anywhere fancier. Come hungry because Edmonds has great food. Then make an afternoon out of wandering downtown before heading toward the waterfront for sunset.

Poulsbo

website | area: Kitsap Peninsula (get directions) | best for: waterfront strolling, Scandinavian charm, and local shops

Poulsbo leans into its Norwegian roots, and it’s adorable for it. Grab a pastry at the bakery, wander the little marina, and soak up a town that feels like a European village landed on Liberty Bay. It’s especially fun as a food-focused day trip, since you can easily bounce between bakeries, cafes, breweries, and local shops without moving your car.

Skagit and Whatcom County

website | area: Skagit & Whatcom County (get directions) | best for: scenic drives, small towns, farmland, and mountain views

These areas are your gateway to the North Cascades and the San Juans, and it’s two of my favorite hidden gems in Washington state worth lingering in on the way. The Skagit Valley tulip fields explode with color each spring, and small towns like La Conner and Bellingham anchor a whole region of farms, water, and mountains.

There’s a lot of things to do in Skagit County, including a great food scene. Use my Bellingham guide and things to do in Lynden and Blaine roundups to plan your adventure.

Pro tip: The tulips draw big crowds on spring weekends. Go on a weekday morning if you can swing it. Or better yet, visit other times of year!

Vashon Island

website | area: Puget Sound (get directions) | best for: beaches, local art, and laid-back island charm

Out of all the islands near Seattle, Vashon is the most underrated. It’s an artsy, unhurried island a short ferry from West Seattle, and most tourists never make the hop. Think farm stands, studios, and a genuinely local pace. Bring a car so you can explore beyond the town center, stopping at beaches, roadside stands, and whatever local shop or gallery catches your eye along the way. There are also a bunch of great Vashon restaurants, so go hungry!

Lopez Island

website | area: San Juan Islands (get directions) | best for: cycling, quiet beaches, and laid-back island exploring

Out of all the San Juan Islands, Lopez is the quiet, flat, bike-friendly one, and locals call it “the friendly isle” for a reason. It’s my pick when I want the islands without the summer bustle of Friday Harbor. Pack a bike or rent one since you’re there, then spend the day hopping between beaches, farms, and quiet stretches of coastline.

Lummi Island

website | area: Whatcom County (get directions) | best for: quiet beaches, scenic drives, and a peaceful island escape

Tiny Lummi Island is reached by a short county ferry from near Bellingham, and it’s home to some of the most renowned reefnet-caught salmon in the Pacific Northwest. It’s small, serene, and exactly the kind of spot most travelers miss. This isn’t an island you visit with a packed sightseeing itinerary; come to slow down, explore the shoreline, and enjoy having very little you need to do.

Fort Worden and the Triangle of Fire

website | area: Port Townsend & Admiralty Inlet (get directions) | best for: military history, coastal scenery, and historic forts

History buffs should visit these hidden gems in Washington state. The old coastal defense forts guarding Puget Sound, known as the Triangle of Fire, let you explore hollow concrete gun batteries tucked into several state parks like Fort Worden in Port Townsend, Fort Flagler also in Port Townsend, and Fort Casey on Whidbey Island. Kids love the tunnels, and the views over the water are stunning.

Pro tip: Bring a flashlight or headlamp for the dark battery tunnels, and remember these sit in state parks, so you’ll need a Discover Pass to park.

Winthrop and the Methow Valley

website | area: North Cascades (get directions) | best for: mountain scenery, outdoor adventures, and Old West charm

Winthrop is an Old West-themed town in the Methow Valley, and in winter, it becomes a cross-country skiing haven far from the big resort crowds. The valley has one of the largest groomed Nordic trail networks in North America, and it stays refreshingly quiet.

Lake Chelan and Yakima Valley wine country

website | area: Central Washington (get directions) | best for: wine tasting, vineyard views, and scenic weekend getaways

Everyone races to Walla Walla, but Lake Chelan and Yakima Valley pour just as beautifully with a fraction of the fuss as other PNW wine regions. Chelan pairs tasting rooms with a gorgeous glacial lake, and Yakima Valley is the workhorse behind a huge share of Washington’s grapes. As a licensed travel agent, this is exactly the kind of swap I love making for clients who want the experience without the crowds.

Alternative cities to Seattle: Olympia, Tacoma, Spokane, and Vancouver

area: statewide | best for: city trips without the crowds

If you’ve done Seattle, give its underrated cousins a turn. Our state capital Olympia is quirky and walkable, Tacoma has a knockout glass-art and food scene, Spokane anchors the whole eastern side of the state with its riverfront, and Vancouver, WA, sits right on the Columbia with easy access to the Gorge. Each one is a real city with real character, minus the Pike Place crush.

Abandoned places and ghost towns

area: statewide | best for: history and photography | best season: spring and fall

Okay, this is my slightly nerdy favorite category. Washington state is dotted with old mining towns and abandoned spots that make for a genuinely eerie, fascinating detour. I went deep on these in my guide to abandoned places in Washington, so start there for the full list of abandoned hidden gems in Washington state.

Tips for visiting Washington’s hidden gems

A few things I’ve learned the hard way that’ll make your trip visiting these hidden gems in Washington state smoother:

  • Grab a Discover Pass before you go. A Discover Pass is required for parking at Washington State Parks and recreation lands managed by the Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) and Department of Natural Resources (DNR). An annual pass is $45, the one-day pass is $10. One pass can be used by two vehicles, but is only valid for one vehicle at a time. Keep in mind national parks like Rainier and Olympic use a separate federal pass, not the Discover Pass, so you may want both.
  • Time your season. Mountain passes and high-elevation spots like Artist Point and the North Cascades Highway are summer-and-early-fall affairs because of snow. Desert spots like Palouse Falls are best in spring when the water’s roaring and the heat hasn’t kicked in. Coastal towns are lovely in summer, and dramatic for storm-watching in winter.
  • Pack for remote. Many of these gems have little or no cell service, limited food, and tiny parking lots. Bring water, snacks, offline maps, and a full tank of gas. Get there early on weekends to beat the crowds and the parking crunch.
  • Pair several gems into one road trip. String the North Cascades, Winthrop, and Lake Chelan into one eastern loop, or combine the ferry towns of Edmonds, Poulsbo, and the islands into a Puget Sound weekend. I have a whole guide on Seattle road trips with route ideas.

And if Seattle is your home base for any of this, my self-guided Seattle food tours are a delicious way to eat like a local between adventures.

Discover Washington state hidden gems with a travel planner

Washington State is more than rainy days and never-ending forests. It’s full of hidden gems that even longtime locals can overlook. From tiny island communities and quirky small towns to waterfalls, dramatic landscapes, and under-the-radar places to eat and drink, there’s always somewhere new to explore.

If mapping all of that out feels like a lot, that’s literally my job! I plan custom Pacific Northwest itineraries through my personal travel planning service, and I’d love to build your route so you spend less time researching and more time actually exploring.
